terms.gloss: loss, harm (the opposite of lucrum, gain)
evidence: Hor. Ep. 1.16.56: damnum est, nōn facinus
terms.comment: To suffer a loss is damnum facere (Plautus, Cicero; Lewis & Short), not to cause one; Lewis & Short give damnum dare, to inflict one, as ante-classical.

terms.gloss: a loss, a sacrifice (properly, throwing goods overboard)
terms.comment: jactūram facere, to suffer a loss or make a sacrifice.
Lewis & Short: several times in Cicero, elsewhere rare. Of a death, as in Pliny.

evidence: Cic. Leg. 1.51: propter damna aut dētrīmenta (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: nam dē mīlle fabae modiīs cum surripis ūnum, damnum est, nōn facinus
phrases.english: for when you steal one peck of beans out of a thousand, it’s a loss, not a crime

phrases.latin: sī citō sustuleris et vāsa parāta erunt, damnī nihil erit ex tempestāte
phrases.english: if you gather them up quickly and have the jars ready, the storm will cost you nothing

phrases.latin: Jactūram gravissimam fēcī, sī jactūra dīcenda est tantī virī āmissiō.
phrases.english: I have suffered a very heavy loss, if the loss of so great a man can be called a loss.

sources: Lewis & Short: damnum · Lewis & Short: jactura · Lewis & Short: amissio · Lewis & Short: detrimentum
